files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller's checklist

Owner: E. Nakamura. Complete in sequence; no skipping ahead.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 that pays in July. If one exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities; note that in some months every payroll run pays in-month.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule and supporting contracts. Check the GL first to avoid a duplicate posting. If it is missing, book June prepaid amortization as ONE combined journal entry. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month a prepaid item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after verifying the GL does not already contain the entry.
5. Verify expense coding on the June vendor bills by comparing the bill documents with the GL. Reclass anything miscoded to the correct expense account.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, after all work in items 1-5 has been booked.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Meridian Basket Inc. began in 2021 when two former retail operations colleagues grew tired of seeing useful, well-designed household goods buried in sprawling online catalogs. They started with a tightly edited collection of pantry organizers, reusable kitchen accessories, desk supplies, and small home-comfort items. The idea was simple: make everyday products easier to choose, describe them honestly, and ship them without fuss.

The company now operates as a small ecommerce business serving individual shoppers as well as a handful of retail and business customers. Its assortment changes with customer feedback rather than trend forecasts alone, and the team favors practical products that are straightforward to store, pack, and replenish.

The staff has the flavor of a close operations crew. Merchandising and marketing trade notes constantly with customer service, while the warehouse team is quick to flag awkward packaging or recurring returns. Finance is lean, detail-oriented, and accustomed to balancing routine close work with the needs of a growing online shop.

Meridian Basket Inc. is currently refining its brand presentation, testing partner marketing, and tightening fulfillment processes. Management remains focused on dependable service, sensible assortment decisions, and the ordinary work of building durable customer relationships.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction

Give Meridian Basket Inc. a cleaner, more recognizable voice without losing the practical tone customers already know. The refresh should emphasize useful products, candid descriptions, and reliable fulfillment rather than lifestyle hype.

## Priorities

- Refresh core brand language and visual guidelines during Q3.
- Run two educational webinars per quarter, built around organization, product care, and small-space routines.
- Test a partner co-marketing pilot with a complementary retailer or service brand.
- Improve product-page storytelling with clearer use cases, packaging details, and customer questions.
- Build reusable email and social content from webinar topics rather than creating isolated campaigns.

## Channel approach

Email remains the primary retention channel. Paid media should support proven product groups and partner activity, while organic social focuses on demonstrations, staff picks, and behind-the-scenes fulfillment content. Avoid broad campaigns that cannot be tied to a defined audience or merchandising goal.

## Measurement

Review webinar attendance quality, partner-referred traffic, repeat engagement, and product-page behavior each quarter. Capture lessons from the Q3 pilot before expanding partner activity in Q4.

Resource allocation remains provisional pending completion of the Q2 close.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# A few handoff notes

E. Nakamura — a few things I learned the hard way here:

- The bank tends to place its own fees and charges near the end of the statement. We book those during close, not during the month, so do not assume the ledger is finished before checking the last part of the statement.
- I was moving too quickly in June, and the expense coding on one or two vendor bills may be wrong. Treat the supporting documents in `bills/` as authoritative and correct the GL to match them.
- The budget was fixed early in the quarter. The one-off June items were never planned, and they are usually the reason the larger budget variances look so pronounced.
- This month, the June 16-30 payroll run pays in the first days of July. The payroll register has the detail, so make sure the timing is reflected in the close.
